docs.title: 🧩 Course Overview
docs.text:
Welcome to the Data Structures and Algorithms 1 (DSA 1) Lab. This website provides all your lab materials, including:

  • Step-by-step tutorials and lecture slides
  • Programming exercises and challenges
  • Sample solutions and best practices
  • Tools, setup, and submission instructions

All labs are taught using the C programming language, focusing on:

  • Clear and structured problem-solving
  • Efficient coding practices
  • Understanding the link between algorithms and implementation

docs.title: 🌱 Git & GitHub: Your Lab Companion
docs.text: Welcome to your complete guide for using Git and GitHub in the DSA 1 Lab! This guide will walk you through everything from installation to submitting your assignments with confidence.

docs.title: 🧠 What Are Git and GitHub?
docs.text:
Tool Role in Your Lab Work Git Your local time machine - tracks every change you make to your code files on your computer GitHub Your online submission folder - stores your code in the cloud and lets instructors see your work

Think of Git as your personal notebook, and GitHub as the teacher's mailbox where you submit assignments.

docs.title: 🪟 On Windows
docs.text:
1. Download from git-scm.com
  2. Run the installer → Keep all default options
  3. Choose "Visual Studio Code" as default editor if prompted
  4. Complete installation

docs.title: 🍎 On macOS
docs.text:
xcode-select --install

Or using Homebrew:

brew install git

docs.title: 🐧 On Linux
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install git

Verify installation:

git --version

docs.title: 🔧 Step 2: Configure Git (One-Time Setup)
docs.text:
git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "your-email@usthb.dz"

This connects your work to your identity - like writing your name on your lab copies.

docs.title: 🚀 How to Complete and Submit Assignments
📥 Step 3: Get Your Assignment Repository
docs.text:
1. Click the GitHub Classroom link provided for each lab
  2. Select your identifier from the roster list
  3. Accept the assignment - GitHub creates your private repository
  4. Clone it to your computer: 
git clone https://github.com/USTHB-DSA1/lab1-yourusername.git
cd lab1-yourusername

docs.title: 💻 Step 4: Work on Your Code
docs.text:
1. Open the folder in VS Code or your preferred editor
  2. Write and test your C programs locally
  3. Save your files regularly

docs.title: 📤 Step 5: Submit Your Work
docs.text:
When you've completed an exercise (or want to save progress):

# Step 1: Add all changed files to "staging area"
git add .

# Step 2: Save your changes with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Completed exercise 1: Fibonacci sequence"

# Step 3: Upload to GitHub (submit your work)
git push origin main

💡 Pro Tip: You can push multiple times! Each push updates your submission.

docs.title: 🎯 Complete Assignment Workflow Example
docs.text:
Let's walk through Lab 1 - Exercise 8:

# 1. Get your assignment (using the URL from Step 3)
git clone https://github.com/DSA1-USTHB/lab1-assignment-exercise8-manel589.git
cd lab1-assignment-exercise8-manel589

# 2. Write code in main.c, test it locally
gcc main.c -o program
./program

# 3. When exercise is working, submit it
git add .
git commit -m "Solved exercise 8: Hello World program"
git push origin main

# 4. Continue with next exercise...
# Edit main.c for exercise 2
git add .
git commit -m "Completed exercise 2: Calculator functions"  
git push origin main

docs.title: 🔄 Keeping Your Work Updated
docs.text:
If the instructor adds new materials or corrections:

# Get the latest updates
git pull origin main

Always do this before starting a new work session.

docs.title: 🌐 Alternative: GitHub Web Editor
docs.text:
For quick fixes or emergencies, you can edit directly on GitHub:

  1. Go to your repository on GitHub.com
  2. Click on any .c file → Edit (pencil icon)
  3. Make changes → Scroll down → Commit changes
  4. Add a message → Click Commit

⚠️ Warning: You can't compile or test code this way - use only for small edits!

docs.title: 🛠️ Essential Git Commands Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Command When to Use It Example git status Check what files you've changed git status git add . Stage all changes for commit git add . git add file.c Stage specific file only git add main.c git commit -m "msg" Save changes with description git commit -m "Fixed bug" git push Upload to GitHub git push git pull Download updates git pull git log See your commit history git log

docs.title: ✅ Do:"
docs.text:
• Commit after each working exercise
  • Write clear commit messages: "Added factorial function" not "fixed stuff"
  • Test your code before pushing
  • Pull updates before starting work
  • Push regularly - don't wait until deadline

docs.title: ❌ Don't:"
docs.text:
• Edit files directly on GitHub (except small fixes)
  • Forget to compile and test locally
  • Use vague commit messages
  • Wait until the last minute to push

docs.title: 🆘 Troubleshooting Common Issues
docs.text: Problem Solution git push asks for password Use GitHub Personal Access Token git pull has conflicts Contact instructor - don't try to resolve complex conflicts alone Can't clone repository Check your internet and the repository URL Files not showing on GitHub Make sure you did git add and git push

docs.title: 📝 Submission Checklist
docs.text:
Before each lab deadline, verify:

  • ☐ All exercises are committed with clear messages
  • ☐ Code compiles without errors
  • ☐ Final version is pushed to GitHub
  • ☐ You can see your code on GitHub.com
  • ☐ All required files are present

docs.title: 🎉 You're Ready!"
docs.text:
You now have everything needed to manage and submit your lab work efficiently. Remember: commit often, push regularly, and test always.

Next: Start with Lab 1: Basic C Concepts and apply your new Git skills!

docs.title: ⚙️ Environment Setup Guide
docs.text:
Welcome to your first step in the DSA 1 adventure! 🚀 Before diving into coding and solving real problems, let’s prepare your machine for success.

This setup guide will walk you through everything you need to start programming in C, from installing your compiler to testing your very first “Hello World” program.

docs.title: 🧩 1. What Is a Compiler?
docs.text:
A compiler is like a translator 🗣️ — it converts the code you write (in C language) into something your computer can actually understand and run.

We’ll use GCC (GNU Compiler Collection) — one of the most popular and reliable C compilers in the world.

You’ll write your code → compile it with GCC → run your program. Simple and powerful.

docs.title: 🔹 On Windows (using MinGW)
docs.text:
1. Go to the MinGW-w64 Download Page
  2. Download the installer (mingw-get-setup.exe)
  3. Run the installer and follow these steps:
  4. Click "Install"
  5. Choose installation directory (default C:\MinGW is fine)
  6. Wait for download and installation
  7. Install Required Packages:
  8. Open MinGW Installation Manager
  9. In the left panel, select All Packages → MinGW → MinGW Base System

  10. Right-click and "Mark for Installation" on:

    • mingw32-base
    • mingw32-gcc-g++
    • mingw32-gdb

  11. Apply Changes:

  12. Go to top menu: Installation → Apply Changes
  13. Click "Apply" and wait for installation to complete

  14. Close MinGW Installation Manager

  15. Add to PATH:

  16. Find your MinGW bin folder (usually C:\MinGW\bin)
  17. Search "Environment Variables" in Start menu
  18. Click "Environment Variables"
  19. Under "System Variables", find "Path", click "Edit"
  20. Click "New" and add: C:\MinGW\bin

  21. Click OK to close all dialogs

  22. Verify Installation:

  23. Open new Command Prompt (important: restart if already open)
  24. Type:
gcc --version

✅ You should see version information — congratulations, GCC is ready!

docs.title: 🔹 On macOS
docs.text:
Just open Terminal and type:

xcode-select --install

This installs Apple’s developer tools, including GCC. Then verify it:

gcc --version

docs.title: 🔹 On Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
docs.text:
Run this in your terminal:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential

Then verify:

gcc --version

Done! 🎉

docs.title: 🧠 3. Choose Your Code Editor
docs.text:
You’ll need a place to write your code — that’s your text editor or IDE (Integrated Development Environment).

Here are your top options:

Editor Description Download VS Code Modern, lightweight, with tons of extensions and built-in terminal. Download VS Code Code::Blocks Classic beginner-friendly IDE that comes with a compiler (optional). Download Code::Blocks CLion (JetBrains) Professional C/C++ IDE, free for students. Download CLion Dev C++ Simple and lightweight IDE for Windows. Download Dev C++

💡 Recommended: VS Code — it’s clean, customizable, and perfect for C beginners.

docs.title: 🔍 4. Testing Your Setup
docs.text:
Let’s see if your environment is ready!

  1. Open your editor or terminal.

  2. Create a file called hello.c and paste this code:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    printf("Hello, DSA 1 Lab!\n");
    return 0;
}
  1. Save the file, then compile and run it:
gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello

If you see this:

Hello, DSA 1 Lab!

🎉 You’ve done it! Your C environment is ready for action.

docs.title: 🧰 5. How It All Works (Behind the Scenes)
docs.text:
Here’s a quick breakdown of what just happened:

Step What It Does gcc hello.c -o hello Compiles your C file into an executable named hello ./hello Runs your compiled program printf() Displays output text in the terminal return 0; Tells the computer your program ran successfully

Understanding this basic flow is key — every C program you’ll write follows this same pattern!

docs.title: ⚡ Common Issues & Fixes
docs.text: Problem Cause Solution 'gcc' is not recognized Compiler not added to PATH Reinstall MinGW or add bin folder manually File not found Wrong directory Use cd to move into your code’s folder Program doesn’t run Missing ./ on Unix/macOS Run as ./program_name Compilation errors Syntax mistakes Check your code for typos or missing semicolons

to learn how we’ll collaborate, submit assignments, and track your progress!

docs.title: 📚 Exercise Overview
docs.text:
These exercises are designed to reinforce the fundamental concepts covered in Lab 1:

  • Variable declarations and initialization
  • Arithmetic operations
  • Mathematical functions
  • Type casting
  • Input/output operations
  • Formula implementation

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Ask the user to enter the radius of a circle. Compute and display both the area and circumference.

Formulas:

  • Area = π × r²
  • Circumference = 2 × π × r

Use: π = 3.14159265359

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter the radius of the circle: 5

=== Circle Properties ===
Radius: 5.00
Area: 78.54
Circumference: 31.42

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Use #define or const for PI
  • Display results with 2 decimal places
  • Handle decimal radius values

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Include math.h for the pow() function (or use r * r)
  2. Use %f format specifier for float/double
  3. Use %.2f to display 2 decimal places
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

int main() {
    const double PI = 3.14159265359;
    double radius, area, circumference;

    // Input
    printf("Enter the radius of the circle: ");
    scanf("%lf", &radius);

    // Calculations
    area = PI * radius * radius;  // Or: PI * pow(radius, 2)
    circumference = 2 * PI * radius;

    // Output
    printf("\n=== Circle Properties ===\n");
    printf("Radius: %.2f\n", radius);
    printf("Area: %.2f\n", area);
    printf("Circumference: %.2f\n", circumference);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Ask for an amount in Algerian Dinar (DZD) and convert it to USD, EUR, and GBP using fixed exchange rates.

Exchange Rates:

  • 1 USD = 134 DZD
  • 1 EUR = 145 DZD
  • 1 GBP = 165 DZD

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter amount in DZD: 10000

=== Currency Conversion ===
10000.00 DZD =
  74.63 USD
  68.97 EUR
  60.61 GBP

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Use constants for exchange rates
  • Display all currencies with 2 decimal places
  • Handle large amounts correctly

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. To convert DZD to USD: usd = dzd / rate_usd
  2. Division gives you the foreign currency amount
  3. Use const double for exchange rates
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>

// Define exchange rates (1 unit = X DZD)
const double USD_RATE = 134.0;
const double EUR_RATE = 145.0;
const double GBP_RATE = 165.0;

int main() {
    double dzd, usd, eur, gbp;

    // Input
    printf("Enter amount in DZD: ");
    scanf("%lf", &dzd);

    // Conversions
    usd = dzd / USD_RATE;
    eur = dzd / EUR_RATE;
    gbp = dzd / GBP_RATE;

    // Output
    printf("\n=== Currency Conversion ===\n");
    printf("%.2f DZD =\n", dzd);
    printf("  %.2f USD\n", usd);
    printf("  %.2f EUR\n", eur);
    printf("  %.2f GBP\n", gbp);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Ask the user to input their height (in meters) and weight (in kilograms), then compute and display their BMI.

Formula:

BMI = weight / (height × height)

BMI Categories:

  • Underweight: BMI < 18.5
  • Normal weight: 18.5 ≤ BMI < 25
  • Overweight: 25 ≤ BMI < 30
  • Obese: BMI ≥ 30

(We'll add category display next week with conditionals!)

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter your weight (kg): 70
Enter your height (m): 1.75

=== BMI Calculator ===
Weight: 70.00 kg
Height: 1.75 m
Your BMI: 22.86

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Accept decimal values for height and weight
  • Display BMI with 2 decimal places
  • Handle height in meters (not centimeters)

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. BMI formula uses height in meters
  2. height × height can be written as height * height or pow(height, 2)
  3. Use double for better precision
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    double weight, height, bmi;

    // Input
    printf("Enter your weight (kg): ");
    scanf("%lf", &weight);

    printf("Enter your height (m): ");
    scanf("%lf", &height);

    // Calculate BMI
    bmi = weight / (height * height);

    // Output
    printf("\n=== BMI Calculator ===\n");
    printf("Weight: %.2f kg\n", weight);
    printf("Height: %.2f m\n", height);
    printf("Your BMI: %.2f\n", bmi);

    // Note: We'll add category interpretation next week!
    printf("\nBMI Categories:\n");
    printf("  < 18.5: Underweight\n");
    printf("  18.5-24.9: Normal weight\n");
    printf("  25.0-29.9: Overweight\n");
    printf("  >= 30.0: Obese\n");

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Input two points in a 2D plane (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), then compute the Euclidean distance between them.

Formula:

distance = √[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²]

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter coordinates of point 1 (x1 y1): 0 0
Enter coordinates of point 2 (x2 y2): 3 4

=== Distance Calculator ===
Point 1: (0.00, 0.00)
Point 2: (3.00, 4.00)
Distance: 5.00

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Use sqrt() function from math.h
  • Display coordinates and distance with 2 decimal places
  • Handle negative coordinates

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Remember: (x₂ - x₁)² = (x2 - x1) * (x2 - x1) or pow(x2 - x1, 2)
  2. Must include math.h for sqrt()
  3. Compile with -lm flag on Linux/Mac
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

int main() {
    double x1, y1, x2, y2;
    double distance;

    // Input first point
    printf("Enter coordinates of point 1 (x1 y1): ");
    scanf("%lf %lf", &x1, &y1);

    // Input second point
    printf("Enter coordinates of point 2 (x2 y2): ");
    scanf("%lf %lf", &x2, &y2);

    // Calculate distance
    // Method 1: Using separate calculations
    double dx = x2 - x1;  // Difference in x
    double dy = y2 - y1;  // Difference in y
    distance = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);

    // Method 2: All in one line
    // distance = sqrt(pow(x2 - x1, 2) + pow(y2 - y1, 2));

    // Output
    printf("\n=== Distance Calculator ===\n");
    printf("Point 1: (%.2f, %.2f)\n", x1, y1);
    printf("Point 2: (%.2f, %.2f)\n", x2, y2);
    printf("Distance: %.2f\n", distance);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Ask the user to input a duration in seconds, then compute and display the equivalent hours, minutes, and remaining seconds.

Example: 3665 seconds = 1 hour, 1 minute, 5 seconds

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter duration in seconds: 3665

=== Time Conversion ===
Total seconds: 3665
Formatted: 1:01:05
(1 hours, 1 minutes, 5 seconds)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Use integer division and modulus operators
  • Format output as H:MM:SS
  • Handle large values (e.g., 86400 seconds = 1 day)

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Hours = seconds / 3600
  2. Remaining after hours = seconds % 3600
  3. Minutes = remaining / 60
  4. Seconds = remaining % 60
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int totalSeconds, hours, minutes, seconds, remaining;

    // Input
    printf("Enter duration in seconds: ");
    scanf("%d", &totalSeconds);

    // Calculations
    hours = totalSeconds / 3600;              // 3600 seconds = 1 hour
    remaining = totalSeconds % 3600;          // Leftover after extracting hours

    minutes = remaining / 60;                 // 60 seconds = 1 minute
    seconds = remaining % 60;                 // Leftover seconds

    // Output
    printf("\n=== Time Conversion ===\n");
    printf("Total seconds: %d\n", totalSeconds);
    printf("Formatted: %d:%02d:%02d\n", hours, minutes, seconds);
    printf("(%d hours, %d minutes, %d seconds)\n", hours, minutes, seconds);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Exercise 6: Elapsed Time Between Two Clock Times ⭐⭐⭐
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Ask for two times: start time (h₁, m₁, s₁) and end time (h₂, m₂, s₂). Compute and display the total elapsed time in hours, minutes, and seconds.

Assumption: End time is always after start time (same day).

docs.title: Sample Input/Output
docs.text:
Enter start time (hours minutes seconds): 10 30 45
Enter end time (hours minutes seconds): 14 45 20

=== Elapsed Time Calculator ===
Start: 10:30:45
End:   14:45:20
Elapsed: 4:14:35
(4 hours, 14 minutes, 35 seconds)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Handle cases where seconds/minutes need borrowing
  • Display in H:MM:SS format
  • Validate that end time > start time (for now, just assume it is)

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Convert both times to total seconds
  2. Calculate difference in seconds
  3. Convert difference back to H:M:S format
  4. Reuse logic from Exercise 5!
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int h1, m1, s1;  // Start time
    int h2, m2, s2;  // End time
    int startSeconds, endSeconds, elapsedSeconds;
    int hours, minutes, seconds, remaining;

    // Input start time
    printf("Enter start time (hours minutes seconds): ");
    scanf("%d %d %d", &h1, &m1, &s1);

    // Input end time
    printf("Enter end time (hours minutes seconds): ");
    scanf("%d %d %d", &h2, &m2, &s2);

    // Convert both times to total seconds
    startSeconds = h1 * 3600 + m1 * 60 + s1;
    endSeconds = h2 * 3600 + m2 * 60 + s2;

    // Calculate elapsed time
    elapsedSeconds = endSeconds - startSeconds;

    // Convert elapsed seconds back to H:M:S
    hours = elapsedSeconds / 3600;
    remaining = elapsedSeconds % 3600;
    minutes = remaining / 60;
    seconds = remaining % 60;

    // Output
    printf("\n=== Elapsed Time Calculator ===\n");
    printf("Start: %02d:%02d:%02d\n", h1, m1, s1);
    printf("End:   %02d:%02d:%02d\n", h2, m2, s2);
    printf("Elapsed: %d:%02d:%02d\n", hours, minutes, seconds);
    printf("(%d hours, %d minutes, %d seconds)\n", hours, minutes, seconds);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem: Road Trip Budget Calculator
docs.text: Create a program that calculates fuel consumption, costs, and trip details for a journey.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Your program asks for:

  1. Distance to travel (km)
  2. Vehicle fuel consumption (L/100km)
  3. Fuel price per liter (DA)
  4. Average speed (km/h)
  5. Number of passengers

docs.title: Calculate and Display
docs.text: Your program must calculate these 7 values:

docs.title: 1. Total fuel needed (liters)
docs.text: Total Fuel = (Distance / 100) × Fuel Consumption

docs.title: 2. Total fuel cost (DA)
docs.text: Total Cost = Total Fuel × Price per Liter

docs.title: 3. Cost per passenger (DA)
docs.text: Cost per Passenger = Total Cost / Number of Passengers

docs.title: 4. Trip duration (hours and minutes)
docs.text:
Hours = Distance / Speed
Minutes = (Distance % Speed) * 60 / Speed

docs.title: 5. Cost per kilometer (DA/km)
docs.text: Cost per km = Total Cost / Distance

docs.title: 6. Number of fuel stops
docs.text:
Assume tank capacity = 50 liters
Stops = how many times you need to refuel
Use ceil() function from math.h

docs.title: 7. CO₂ emissions (kg)
docs.text:
CO₂ = Total Fuel × 2.31
(2.31 kg CO₂ per liter of gasoline)

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
Enter distance to travel (km): 450
Enter vehicle fuel consumption (L/100km): 7.5
Enter fuel price per liter (DA): 45.50
Enter average speed (km/h): 110
Enter number of passengers: 4

=== Trip Calculation ===
Distance: 450 km
Estimated Duration: 4h 05min

Fuel Consumption:
  Total Fuel Needed: 33.75 L
  Total Cost: 1535.63 DA
  Cost per km: 3.41 DA
  Cost per passenger: 383.91 DA

Fuel Stops Required: 0 stops
(Tank capacity: 50 L)

Environmental Impact:
  CO2 Emissions: 77.96 kg

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Use #include <math.h> for ceil() function
  • Display numbers with 2 decimal places (.2f)
  • Compile with: gcc -Wall homework.c -lm -o homework
  • Name your file: road_trip.c

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
1. Accept GitHub Classroom assignment: Link
  2. Clone your repository
  3. Write your code in road_trip.c
  4. Test with the example above

  5. Commit and push:

    git add road_trip.c
git commit -m "Complete road trip calculator"
git push

docs.title: 🚀 Welcome to C Programming
docs.text:
C is a general-purpose programming language created in 1972 by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs. It's the foundation of many modern languages including C++, Java, and Python and is still widely used today because it's:

  • Fast and efficient — gives you direct access to memory and hardware.
  • Powerful and flexible — used in OS kernels (Linux, Windows), databases, and embedded systems.
  • Fundamental for learning algorithms and data structures.

Learning C helps you understand how computers really work — memory, logic, and performance at their core.

docs.title: 🤔 Why C Still Matters in 2025
docs.text:
Historical Significance:

  • C was designed to rewrite the UNIX operating system, making it portable across different machines
  • Before C, operating systems were written in assembly language — tied to specific hardware
  • C introduced the revolutionary concept of "write once, compile anywhere"

Modern Relevance:

  • Operating Systems: Linux kernel, Windows NT kernel, macOS core components
  • Embedded Systems: Your smartphone, car, microwave — all run C code
  • Performance-Critical Applications: Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), game engines, compilers
  • IoT and Edge Computing: Resource-constrained devices need C's efficiency

Why Learn C First?

  1. No magic, no hidden complexity — every operation is explicit
  2. Teaches memory management — you understand what happens "under the hood"
  3. Foundation for understanding higher-level languages — Java's JVM, Python's CPython interpreter are written in C
  4. Algorithmic thinking — forces you to think about efficiency and resources

docs.title: The Philosophy of C
docs.text:
C follows the principle: "Trust the programmer."

  • Gives you complete control but expects responsibility
  • Doesn't protect you from mistakes — you learn by debugging
  • Minimal runtime overhead — your code runs close to hardware speed

docs.title: What Makes C Different?
docs.text: Aspect C Higher-Level Languages Memory Management Manual (you allocate/free) Automatic (garbage collection) Performance Direct hardware access Runtime interpretation overhead Abstraction Level Low-level (close to machine) High-level (abstract concepts) Compilation Compiles to native code Often interpreted or JIT compiled Learning Curve Steeper (more concepts) Gentler (many details hidden)

docs.title: Real-World Impact
docs.text:
Example: Why is Linux written in C?

  • Performance: Kernel needs to be fast — C compiles to efficient machine code
  • Portability: Linux runs on everything from phones to supercomputers
  • Control: Direct hardware access without abstraction layers
  • Predictability: No unexpected garbage collection pauses

docs.title: Understanding the Compilation Process
docs.text:
Before we write code, let's understand what happens when you "run" a C program:

Source Code (.c) → Preprocessor → Compiler → Assembler → Linker → Executable
  1. Preprocessor — Handles #include and #define directives
  2. Compiler — Converts C code to assembly language
  3. Assembler — Converts assembly to machine code (object files)
  4. Linker — Combines object files with libraries into final executable

docs.title: Code Editors:
docs.text:
• Code::Blocks
  • Visual Studio Code
  • Dev-C++

docs.title: First Compilation
docs.text:
# Compile a program
gcc hello.c -o hello

# With warnings enabled (ALWAYS do this!)
gcc -Wall -Wextra hello.c -o hello

# Run the program
./hello

What do these flags mean?

  • -Wall — Enable all common warnings
  • -Wextra — Enable extra warnings
  • -o hello — Name the output file "hello"
  • -lm — Link math library (needed for math.h functions)

Why enable warnings?

  • Catches potential bugs before runtime
  • Teaches you good practices
  • Professional code always compiles without warnings

docs.title: 🧩 Anatomy of a Simple C Program
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>   // Include standard input/output library

int main() {         // Program execution starts here
    printf("Hello, world!\n");  // Display output
    return 0;        // End program successfully
}

docs.title: #include <stdio.h>
docs.text:
What it does:

  • Includes the Standard Input/Output header file
  • Contains declarations for printf(), scanf(), etc.

Why angle brackets < >?

  • Tells compiler to look in system directories
  • Use quotes " " for your own header files: #include "myheader.h"

What's in stdio.h?

  • Function declarations (prototypes)
  • Macro definitions
  • Type definitions

docs.title: int main()
docs.text:
Why int?

  • main() returns an integer to the operating system
  • 0 means success, non-zero means error
  • This is how shell scripts check if commands succeeded

The Operating System Connection:

int main() {
    // Your code here
    return 0;  // Tell OS: "Everything went fine"
}

When you run ./program, the OS:

  1. Loads your executable into memory
  2. Calls main()
  3. Receives the return value
  4. Uses it to determine if program succeeded

docs.title: printf("Hello, world!\n");
docs.text:
How does printf work?

  • It's a variadic function — takes variable number of arguments
  • Interprets format specifiers at runtime
  • Sends output to standard output (stdout)

Why the \n?

  • Newline character — moves cursor to next line
  • This is called "line buffering"

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
// Single-line comment — ignored by compiler

/*
 * Multi-line comment
 * Can span multiple lines
 * Often used for documentation
 */

Best Practices:

  • Comment why, not what — code shows what you're doing
  • Bad: x = x + 1; // Increment x
  • Good: x++; // Move to next array position after processing

docs.title: Data Types: Why Do We Need Them?
docs.text:
The Problem: Memory is just a sequence of bytes (0s and 1s). How does the computer know if 01000001 means:

  • The number 65?
  • The letter 'A'?
  • Part of a larger number?

The Solution: Data Types Types tell the compiler:

  1. How much memory to allocate
  2. How to interpret the bits
  3. What operations are valid

docs.title: Integer Types
docs.text:
Type Size Range Why Use It? char 1 byte -128 to 127 Single characters, small numbers short 2 bytes -32,768 to 32,767 When you need to save memory int 4 bytes -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 Default choice for integers long 8 bytes Very large numbers Big data, timestamps, IDs long long 8 bytes Guaranteed 64-bit Portable large integers

unsigned variants:

unsigned int age = 25;  // Only positive: 0 to 4,294,967,295

Why unsigned?

  • Doubles the positive range
  • Use when negative values are impossible (age, count, array indices)
  • Bit operations often use unsigned

Common Pitfall:

unsigned int x = 0;
x = x - 1;  // Underflow! x is now 4,294,967,295 (wraps around)

docs.title: Floating-Point Types
docs.text:
Type Size Precision Why Use It? float 4 bytes ~7 digits Graphics, games (where speed > precision) double 8 bytes ~15 digits Scientific calculations, default choice long double 10-16 bytes ~19 digits Extreme precision needs

Why are floats "approximate"? Floats use IEEE 754 format — stores numbers in scientific notation:

3.14159 = 3.14159 × 10^0
        = Sign × Mantissa × 2^Exponent

Consequence: Some numbers can't be represented exactly

float x = 0.1 + 0.2;  // x might be 0.30000001, not exactly 0.3!

When to use double vs float?

  • Use double by default — modern CPUs are optimized for it
  • Use float when memory is critical (large arrays, embedded systems)
  • Never use float for money — use integers (cents instead of dollars)

docs.title: Character Type
docs.text:
char grade = 'A';  // Single quotes for characters!

What's really stored?

  • ASCII code: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66, etc.
  • You can do arithmetic: 'A' + 1 = 'B'

docs.title: Declaration vs Initialization
docs.text:
int age;           // Declaration — reserves memory
age = 20;          // Initialization — stores value

int height = 175;  // Declaration + Initialization

What happens in memory?

Declaration:
int age;
┌─────┐
│  ?  │  ← Garbage value (whatever was there before)
└─────┘

Initialization:
age = 20;
┌─────┐
│ 20  │  ← Known value
└─────┘

docs.title: The Danger of Uninitialized Variables
docs.text:
int x;              // Declared but not initialized
printf("%d", x);    // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR! Prints garbage

Why is this dangerous?

  • May print 0, 42, -1573829, or crash
  • Depends on what was previously in that memory location
  • Always initialize variables before use, or ensure they're assigned a value before being read!

docs.title: Multiple Declarations
docs.text:
int a, b, c;           // All uninitialized
int x = 1, y = 2, z;   // x=1, y=2, z is garbage!

Best Practice:

int a = 0;  // One per line, always initialize
int b = 0;
int c = 0;

docs.title: Why Use Constants?
docs.text:
Bad Code:

area = 3.14159 * radius * radius;
circumference = 2 * 3.14159 * radius;
volume = (4.0 / 3.0) * 3.14159 * radius * radius * radius;
// What if you type 3.14159 wrong somewhere?

Good Code:

const double PI = 3.14159265359;
area = PI * radius * radius;
circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
volume = (4.0 / 3.0) * PI * radius * radius * radius;

docs.title: 1. Preprocessor Directive
docs.text:
#define PI 3.14159
#define MAX_STUDENTS 100

How it works:

  • Preprocessor literally replaces text before compilation
  • #define PI 3.14159 → Every PI becomes 3.14159
  • No type checking
  • No memory allocated
  • No semicolon!

When to use:

  • Simple value substitutions
  • Conditional compilation
  • Macro functions

docs.title: 2. Const Keyword
docs.text:
const double PI = 3.14159265359;
const int MAX_STUDENTS = 100;

How it works:

  • Creates a read-only variable
  • Type-checked by compiler
  • Takes memory space
  • Can't be modified

When to use:

  • Prefer this for modern C code
  • When you need type safety
  • When you need to pass by reference

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Feature #define const Type checking No Yes Debugger visibility No Yes Memory usage None Yes (tiny) Scope Global Block/function Preferred? Legacy code Modern C

docs.title: Understanding Standard I/O
docs.text:
Programs interact with three streams:

  • stdin (standard input) — keyboard by default
  • stdout (standard output) — terminal/console
  • stderr (standard error) — error messages
Keyboard → stdin → Program → stdout → Screen
                            → stderr → Screen

docs.title: printf() Deep Dive
docs.text:
printf("I am %d years old\n", age);

How it works:

  1. Scans format string for % specifiers
  2. Replaces them with corresponding arguments
  3. Sends result to stdout

Format Specifier Syntax:

%[flags][width][.precision][length]type

Examples:

printf("%d", 42);        // Simple: 42
printf("%5d", 42);       // Width 5:    42
printf("%-5d", 42);      // Left-aligned: 42   
printf("%05d", 42);      // Zero-padded: 00042
printf("%.2f", 3.14159); // 2 decimals: 3.14
printf("%8.2f", 3.14);   // Width 8, 2 decimals:     3.14

docs.title: Common Format Specifiers
docs.text: Specifier Type Example Output %d or %i Signed int -42 %u Unsigned int 42 %f Float/double 3.140000 %lf Double (scanf only!) 3.140000 %c Char A %s String Hello %p Pointer address 0x7ffe5467e044 %x Hex (lowercase) 2a %X Hex (uppercase) 2A %% Literal % %

docs.title: scanf() Deep Dive
docs.text:
int age;
scanf("%d", &age);  // Note the &

Why the & (address-of operator)?

Memory:
┌─────┐
│  ?  │  age lives at address 1000
└─────┘
   ↑
   1000

scanf needs to know WHERE to store input.
&age gives it the address: 1000

Without &:

scanf("%d", age);  // WRONG! Passes value of age (garbage)
                   // scanf tries to write to random memory → CRASH

Reading Multiple Values:

int day, month, year;
scanf("%d %d %d", &day, &month, &year);
// Input: 25 10 2025

Reading Characters (Tricky!):

char ch;
scanf(" %c", &ch);  // Space before %c to skip whitespace!

Why the space?

  • scanf leaves newline in buffer after previous input
  • %c tells it to skip whitespace first

docs.title: Common scanf() Pitfalls
docs.text:
Problem 1: Leftover newlines

int num;
char ch;
scanf("%d", &num);   // User types: 5<Enter>
scanf("%c", &ch);    // Reads <Enter>, not next char!

// Solution:
scanf("%d", &num);
scanf(" %c", &ch);   // Space skips whitespace

Problem 2: Buffer overflow

char name[50];
scanf("%s", name);  // Dangerous if input > 49 chars!

// Safer:
scanf("%49s", name);  // Limit to 49 chars (+ null terminator)

docs.title: The Five Basic Operations
docs.text:
int a = 10, b = 3;

printf("%d\n", a + b);  // 13
printf("%d\n", a - b);  // 7
printf("%d\n", a * b);  // 30
printf("%d\n", a / b);  // 3  ← Integer division!
printf("%d\n", a % b);  // 1  ← Remainder

docs.title: Integer Division: The Source of Many Bugs
docs.text:
The Rule: If both operands are integers, result is integer (truncated, not rounded).

int result = 5 / 2;     // 2 (not 2.5!)
float result = 5 / 2;   // 2.0 (division happens first, then assigned)
float result = 5.0 / 2; // 2.5 (float division)
float result = (float)5 / 2;  // 2.5 (cast one operand)

Why does this happen?

  • Efficiency: Integer division is faster than floating-point
  • Historical: Matches how CPU arithmetic works
  • Predictable: Same behavior across all C compilers

Real-world bug example:

// Calculate average of exam scores
int score1 = 85, score2 = 90, score3 = 78;
int sum = score1 + score2 + score3;  // 253
float average = sum / 3;              // 84.0 (WRONG!)

// Correct:
float average = (float)sum / 3;       // 84.33
// Or:
float average = sum / 3.0;            // 84.33

docs.title: Modulus Operator (%)
docs.text:
What it does: Returns remainder after division

10 % 3 = 1   // 10 ÷ 3 = 3 remainder 1
15 % 4 = 3   // 15 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 3
20 % 5 = 0   // 20 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 0

Common Uses:

  1. Check even/odd:
if (num % 2 == 0) {
    printf("Even");
} else {
    printf("Odd");
}
  1. Cycle through array:
index = (index + 1) % arraySize;  // Wraps around: 0,1,2,0,1,2...
  1. Extract digits:
int lastDigit = num % 10;     // 12345 → 5
num = num / 10;                // 12345 → 1234
  1. Check divisibility:
if (year % 4 == 0) {
    // Might be leap year...
}

Important: Modulus only works with integers!

float x = 7.5 % 2.5;  // COMPILATION ERROR!
float x = fmod(7.5, 2.5);  // Use fmod() for floats

docs.title: Basic Assignment
docs.text: int x = 10;  // Assigns 10 to x

docs.title: Compound Assignment Operators
docs.text:
Instead of:

x = x + 5;
x = x - 3;
x = x * 2;
x = x / 4;
x = x % 3;

Write:

x += 5;  // Same as x = x + 5
x -= 3;  // Same as x = x - 3
x *= 2;  // Same as x = x * 2
x /= 4;  // Same as x = x / 4
x %= 3;  // Same as x = x % 3

Why use compound operators?

  1. Shorter, more readable — less typing
  2. Compiler optimization — sometimes generates faster code
  3. Less error-prone — can't accidentally use wrong variable

docs.title: Increment and Decrement
docs.text:
Post-increment/decrement:

int x = 5;
int y = x++;  // y = 5, then x = 6 (use then increment)

Pre-increment/decrement:

int x = 5;
int y = ++x;  // x = 6, then y = 6 (increment then use)

Visualization:

// Post-increment (x++)
int x = 5;
int y = x++;
// Steps:
// 1. Evaluate x (5)
// 2. Assign to y (y = 5)
// 3. Increment x (x = 6)

// Pre-increment (++x)
int x = 5;
int y = ++x;
// Steps:
// 1. Increment x (x = 6)
// 2. Evaluate x (6)
// 3. Assign to y (y = 6)

When does it matter?

int x = 5;
x++;        // Same as
++x;        // Same as
x += 1;     // Same as
x = x + 1;  // All produce x = 6

// Only matters in expressions:
arr[i++];   // Use i, then increment
arr[++i];   // Increment i, then use

Best Practice: Use standalone when possible to avoid confusion

// Clear:
x++;
doSomething(x);

// Confusing:
doSomething(x++);  // Is x incremented before or after the call?

docs.title: 🎯 Operator Precedence
docs.text:
When you write:

int result = 2 + 3 * 4;

Which happens first, addition or multiplication?

docs.title: Precedence Table (Simplified)
docs.text: Priority Operators Example 1 (Highest) () Parentheses (a + b) 2 ++ -- (prefix) ++x 3 * / % a * b 4 + - a + b 5 (Lowest) = += -= etc. x = 5

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
2 + 3 * 4        // = 2 + 12 = 14 (not 20!)
(2 + 3) * 4      // = 5 * 4 = 20
10 / 2 * 3       // = 5 * 3 = 15 (left to right)
10 - 5 - 2       // = 5 - 2 = 3 (left to right)

Why precedence exists:

  • Matches mathematical conventions (PEMDAS)
  • Makes code less verbose (fewer parentheses needed)
  • Standardized across programming languages

Best Practice: When in doubt, use parentheses!

// Unclear:
result = a + b * c - d / e;

// Clear:
result = a + (b * c) - (d / e);

docs.title: Implicit vs Explicit Casting
docs.text:
Implicit (Automatic):

int x = 5;
float y = x;  // Compiler automatically converts 5 to 5.0

Explicit (Manual):

float x = 7.8;
int y = (int)x;  // You explicitly request conversion to int

docs.title: Type Conversion Rules
docs.text:
Promotion Hierarchy:

char → int → long → float → double

In mixed expressions:

int + float   → float
int + double  → double
float + double → double

Example:

int a = 5;
float b = 2.5;
double result = a + b;  // a promoted to float, then to double
// result = 7.5

docs.title: Common Casting Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Avoiding Integer Division:

int a = 5, b = 2;
float result = a / b;           // 2.0 (WRONG)
float result = (float)a / b;    // 2.5 (CORRECT)
float result = a / (float)b;    // 2.5 (CORRECT)
float result = (float)(a / b);  // 2.0 (TOO LATE!)

2. Truncating Decimals:

float price = 19.99;
int dollars = (int)price;  // 19 (truncates, doesn't round!)

// To round:
int rounded = (int)(price + 0.5);  // 20

3. Character-Number Conversion:

char letter = 'A';
int ascii = (int)letter;  // 65

int code = 65;
char letter = (char)code;  // 'A'

4. Pointer Casting (Advanced):

void* ptr = malloc(100);
int* intPtr = (int*)ptr;  // Cast void pointer to int pointer

docs.title: Dangers of Casting
docs.text:
Loss of Precision:

double pi = 3.14159;
int truncated = (int)pi;  // 3 (lost decimal part forever!)

Overflow:

int large = 50000;
short small = (short)large;  // Might overflow! Undefined behavior

Sign Issues:

int negative = -1;
unsigned int positive = (unsigned)negative;  // 4294967295 (wraps around!)

docs.title: Why We Need math.h
docs.text:
Basic operators (+, -, *, /, %) are limited. For complex math:

#include <math.h>

What math.h provides:

  • Trigonometry (sin, cos, tan)
  • Powers and roots (pow, sqrt)
  • Logarithms (log, log10)
  • Rounding (ceil, floor, round)
  • Constants (M_PI, M_E)

docs.title: Power and Root
docs.text:
double result;
result = pow(2.0, 3.0);   // 8.0 (2³)
result = sqrt(16.0);      // 4.0 (√16)
result = cbrt(27.0);      // 3.0 (∛27)

Why pass doubles?

  • Math functions work with doubles for precision
  • Integers are automatically promoted

docs.title: Rounding Functions
docs.text:
double x = 4.7;
ceil(x);    // 5.0 (rounds up)
floor(x);   // 4.0 (rounds down)
round(x);   // 5.0 (rounds to nearest)
trunc(x);   // 4.0 (removes decimals)

Use cases:

  • ceil(): Calculating number of pages, buckets needed
  • floor(): Converting prices, array indices
  • round(): Statistical rounding
  • trunc(): Like (int) cast but returns double

docs.title: Absolute Value
docs.text:
int abs(int x);         // For integers
float fabs(float x);    // For floats
double fabs(double x);  // For doubles

int x = -42;
int positive = abs(x);  // 42

double y = -3.14;
double positive = fabs(y);  // 3.14

docs.title: Trigonometry (Radians!)
docs.text:
double angle_degrees = 45.0;
double angle_radians = angle_degrees * M_PI / 180.0;

double sine = sin(angle_radians);
double cosine = cos(angle_radians);
double tangent = tan(angle_radians);

Common mistake: Forgetting to convert degrees to radians!

sin(45);  // WRONG! sin expects radians
sin(45 * M_PI / 180);  // CORRECT

docs.title: Compilation with math.h
docs.text:
On Linux/Mac:

gcc program.c -lm -o program

The -lm flag links the math library.

Why is this needed?

  • Math functions are in a separate library (libm.so or libm.a)
  • Linker needs to be told to include it
  • On Windows (most IDEs), this happens automatically

Without -lm:

undefined reference to `sqrt'
undefined reference to `pow'

docs.title:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

int main() {
    double a, b, c;
    double discriminant, root1, root2;

    // Input coefficients
    printf("Enter coefficients (a b c): ");
    scanf("%lf %lf %lf", &a, &b, &c);

    // Calculate discriminant
    discriminant = b * b - 4 * a * c;

    // Calculate roots (assuming real roots)
    root1 = (-b + sqrt(discriminant)) / (2 * a);
    root2 = (-b - sqrt(discriminant)) / (2 * a);

    // Output
    printf("Root 1: %.2f\n", root1);
    printf("Root 2: %.2f\n", root2);

    return 0;
}
Understanding vs Memorizing
docs.text:
Don't just memorize syntax — understand the concepts:

❌ Bad approach: "I need to write scanf("%d", &x) because that's the rule"

✓ Good approach: "scanf needs the memory address where to store input, so I use &"

docs.title: The Three-Step Learning Process
docs.text:
1. Read and Understand
  2. Why does this concept exist?
  3. What problem does it solve?

  4. How is it used in real programs?

  5. Experiment

  6. Modify example code
  7. Try edge cases (what if input is 0? negative? huge?)

  8. Break things intentionally and see what happens

  9. Apply

  10. Write programs from scratch
  11. Solve problems without looking at examples
  12. Explain concepts to others (teaching = learning)

docs.title: Common Beginner Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
1. Forgetting Semicolons
docs.text:
printf("Hello")  // Error: expected ';' before 'return'
return 0;

Why it happens: Coming from Python or other languages without semicolons Solution: Configure editor to highlight missing semicolons

docs.title: 2. Missing & in scanf
docs.text:
int age;
scanf("%d", age);  // Dangerous! Writes to random memory

Why it happens: Confusion about pointers Solution: Remember: scanf needs the address, not the value

docs.title: 3. Integer Division Surprise
docs.text:
float avg = 5 / 2;  // 2.0, not 2.5!

Why it happens: Not understanding type conversion timing Solution: Cast at least one operand (float)5 / 2 or 5.0 / 2

docs.title: 4. Uninitialized Variables
docs.text:
int x;
printf("%d", x);  // Undefined behavior!

Why it happens: Assuming variables default to 0 Solution: Always initialize: int x = 0;

docs.title: 5. Wrong Format Specifier
docs.text:
float pi = 3.14;
printf("%d", pi);  // Garbage output!

Why it happens: Mixing up format codes Solution: Create a reference card:

  • %d = int
  • %f = float/double
  • %c = char
  • %s = string

docs.title: Using printf() for Debugging
docs.text:
The simplest debugging tool:

printf("DEBUG: x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);

Track program flow:

printf("Before calculation\n");
result = complex_formula();
printf("After calculation: result = %f\n", result);

Check variable values:

printf("a=%d b=%d c=%d\n", a, b, c);
calculation();
printf("After: a=%d b=%d c=%d\n", a, b, c);

docs.title: Understanding Compiler Errors
docs.text:
Example error:

error: expected ';' before 'return'

How to read it:

  1. Line number — where error was detected (might be previous line!)
  2. Error type — what went wrong
  3. Context — surrounding code that helps locate issue

Common pattern:

program.c:10:5: error: 'x' undeclared
  • program.c — file name
  • 10 — line number
  • 5 — column number
  • error: — type of message
  • Description — what's wrong

docs.title: Compiler Warning Flags
docs.text:
Compile with warnings enabled:

gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror program.c
  • -Wall — Enable all warnings
  • -Wextra — Extra warnings
  • -Werror — Treat warnings as errors

Why this matters:

int x;
if (x = 5) {  // Warning: assignment in condition
    // ...
}
// Should be: if (x == 5)

Without warnings, this compiles but has a bug!

docs.title: 1. Meaningful Variable Names
docs.text:
// Bad
int x, y, z;
float a, b, c;

// Good
int age, height, weight;
float price, tax, total;

docs.title: 2. Consistent Indentation
docs.text:
// Bad
int main() {
int x = 5;
if (x > 0) {
printf("Positive");
}
return 0;
}

// Good
int main() {
    int x = 5;
    if (x > 0) {
        printf("Positive");
    }
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. One Statement Per Line
docs.text:
// Bad
int x = 5; int y = 10; int z = x + y;

// Good
int x = 5;
int y = 10;
int z = x + y;

docs.title: 4. Spaces Around Operators
docs.text:
// Bad
x=5+3*2;

// Good
x = 5 + 3 * 2;

docs.title: 5. Comments That Add Value
docs.text:
// Bad
x = x + 1;  // Increment x

// Good
x++;  // Move to next student in array

docs.title: Program Structure
docs.text:
Organize your code logically:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

// Constants at the top
#define MAX_SIZE 100
const double PI = 3.14159265359;

int main() {
    // 1. Variable declarations
    int age;
    float height;

    // 2. Input
    printf("Enter age: ");
    scanf("%d", &age);

    // 3. Processing
    float yearsToRetirement = 65 - age;

    // 4. Output
    printf("Years to retirement: %.0f\n", yearsToRetirement);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Testing Your Programs
docs.text:
Test with different inputs:

  1. Normal cases

    • Typical expected values
    • Example: age = 25

  2. Edge cases

    • Minimum/maximum valid values
    • Example: age = 0, age = 120

  3. Invalid inputs

    • What if user enters negative number?
    • What if they enter text instead of number?

  4. Boundary values

    • Just above/below limits
    • Example: age = 64, 65 (retirement age)

Example test plan for average calculator:

Test 1: scores = 85, 90, 78 → expected: 84.33
Test 2: scores = 100, 100, 100 → expected: 100.00
Test 3: scores = 0, 0, 0 → expected: 0.00
Test 4: scores = 33, 34, 33 → expected: 33.33

docs.title: Common Format Specifiers
docs.text:
%d or %i    signed int
%u          unsigned int
%f          float/double (printf)
%lf         double (scanf)
%c          char
%s          string
%p          pointer
%x          hexadecimal
%%          literal %

docs.title: Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
+   addition
-   subtraction
*   multiplication
/   division (integer if both operands are int)
%   modulus (remainder)

docs.title: Assignment Operators
docs.text:
=   simple assignment
+=  add and assign
-=  subtract and assign
*=  multiply and assign
/=  divide and assign
%=  modulus and assign

docs.title: Type Sizes (Typical)
docs.text:
char        1 byte
short       2 bytes
int         4 bytes
long        4-8 bytes
float       4 bytes
double      8 bytes

docs.title: Math Functions (math.h)
docs.text:
pow(x, y)   x raised to y
sqrt(x)     square root
ceil(x)     round up
floor(x)    round down
fabs(x)     absolute value
sin(x)      sine (radians)
cos(x)      cosine (radians)

docs.title: Compilation Commands
docs.text:
# Basic compilation
gcc program.c -o program

# With warnings
gcc -Wall -Wextra program.c -o program

# With math library
gcc program.c -lm -o program

# All together
gcc -Wall -Wextra program.c -lm -o program
